headline: Peconic still running warm — porgies thick around Shelter Island, first bait pushes hint at the turn
subhead: Bay water is holding onto summer while bunker schools start building for the fall run everyone's waiting on.
body_markdown:
The Peconic hasn't gotten the memo that August is ending. Surface temps in the bay are still sitting in that warm, late-summer range, well above what the open Sound and ocean beaches are reading right now, and that lag is exactly why the porgy and fluke bite has stayed dependable while other zones start to wobble. The bay's shallow, protected geometry means it heats faster in spring and holds heat longer into fall — that's the whole reason this fishery runs on its own clock, a week or two ahead of the Sound in May and a week or two behind it when things finally cool off in October. Right now we're still on the summer side of that ledger, and the fishing reflects it.

Nights are starting to dip, though, and that's the thing to watch over the next several days. Cooler overnight air combined with the building moon means tidal flow is picking up, and that increased current is starting to concentrate bait — small bunker pods showing in the back of Three Mile Harbor and Noyack Bay, rain bait working the edges of the Greenport breakwater. Nothing dramatic yet, but it's the same mechanism that eventually triggers the fall striper push through Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip. We flagged this trend last week — said fluke and porgy action would hold steady through the scallop opener with bonito potential building at the inlets — and that's exactly the shape of things right now. No confirmed bonito yet inside Peconic waters, but the ingredients (warm bay water, tightening bait, building current) are lining up the way they usually do before that fish shows.

Porgy fishing remains the strongest, most consistent thing going in this zone. The reefs and rock piles off Shelter Island — Cedar Point, the rips off Hay Beach, and the drop-offs toward Coecles Harbor — are holding heavy numbers of scup in the 10-to-20-foot range, thickest on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing when current is moving but not ripping. Standard high-low rigs with size 6 or 4 hooks, tipped with squid strips or sandworm, are doing the damage, and there's no need to overthink bait presentation right now — the fish are eating anything that sinks with a little movement. Anchoring up-current and letting bait settle into the structure is outproducing constant drifting, since porgies here are holding tight to specific bottom contours rather than roaming.

Fluke are still in the game but showing the softer late-August pattern typical of this time of year — fair, not fast, and increasingly channel-bound as the shallow flats warm past their comfort zone. The deeper cuts through Noyack Bay, the Shelter Island ferry channels, and the mouth of Three Mile Harbor are holding keeper-class fish in 15 to 25 feet, best worked on the last of the outgoing when current stacks bait against the channel edges. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, are taking fish, along with the old standby of squid strip and spearing combos fished on a simple fluke rig with just enough sinker to hold bottom. This is a normal seasonal shift, not a collapse — expect fluke to keep producing on these deeper structures right through September before the real offshore migration pulls them out for good.

Bluefish remain the most aggressive predator in the bay system right now, and they're not subtle about it. Blitzes have been popping along the Orient Point rip and in Gardiners Bay off Cartwright Shoal, usually tied to the same bait pushes bringing bunker into the harbors. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything that throws flash — are getting hit hard when the blitzes surface, typically on a moving tide rather than dead slack. This bluefish activity should track bait density closely through the next couple weeks, and with bunker schools building, there's no reason to expect it to ease up before Labor Day.

Striped bass are present but still in that in-between phase — some fish working the current seams at Plum Gut and the North Race on the tide changes, a few holding around Shelter Island's deeper drop-offs, but nothing like the concentrated fall push that's coming. That trigger is bait density, and the bunker schools in the harbors need another week or two of building before the bass commit in numbers. Bucktails worked slow off the bottom at Plum Gut on the max of either tide are the way to find them right now, along with live bait — peanut bunker under a float — fished tight to structure in Noyack and Three Mile Harbor.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold this same pattern: warm bay water keeping porgies and fluke reliable, bluefish staying active wherever bait concentrates, and stripers slowly building toward the real transition. If the nights keep cooling and that moon-driven current keeps building, the first real signs of the fall run should start showing at Plum Gut and Orient Point within the next week to ten days. Until then, the smart move is working the bay's structure — the Shelter Island reefs, the harbor channels, the rip lines — while the water's still warm enough to keep everything biting.
